stem: A parent asks why an immunocompetent 11-year-old who has never received HPV vaccine should start the series now. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: HPV vaccination is routinely recommended at age 11–12 years because it prevents new HPV infections that can cause cancers later in life; when started at ages 9–14, the routine series is 2 doses 6–12 months apart.
options.B: HPV vaccination should be delayed until adulthood because it works best only after a person has already been exposed to HPV.
options.C: HPV vaccine is used to treat an existing HPV infection, so it is started only after an HPV-related lesion or abnormal screening result develops.
options.D: HPV vaccination is recommended only for girls because HPV-related cancers do not occur in boys or men.

rationale: A is correct. The current CDC child/adolescent immunization schedule notes routine HPV vaccination at age 11–12 years, with vaccination permitted starting at age 9. For people who initiate vaccination at ages 9–14 years, the routine schedule is 2 doses at 0 and 6–12 months; immunocompromised persons require a 3-dose series. CDC also states that HPV vaccination prevents new HPV infections rather than treating existing infection or disease and protects against HPV infections that cause cancers in both females and males. B is incorrect because vaccination is most beneficial before exposure. C reverses prevention and treatment. D is incorrect because HPV causes cancers in both men and women and vaccination is recommended for all preteens.
educational_objective: Explain the cancer-prevention purpose and current routine schedule of HPV vaccination for an immunocompetent preteen, including why vaccination is given before likely HPV exposure and why it applies regardless of sex.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Child Immunization Schedule Notes; Child and Adolescent Immunization Schedule by Age (Compliant); HPV Vaccine Recommendations; Cancers Caused by HPV
source_version_date: Current compliant CDC child/adolescent schedule dated 2025-07-02 and identified by CDC as current in 2026 pursuant to the March 16, 2026 court order; supporting HPV/cancer pages current and accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: Child Immunization Schedule Notes — 'Human papillomavirus vaccination' → 'Routine and catch-up vaccination': routine age 11–12, can start age 9, age 9–14 initiation = 2-dose series at 0 and 6–12 months; HPV Vaccine Recommendations — 'Routine recommendations' and 'Dosing schedule': prevents new infection, does not treat existing disease; Cancers Caused by HPV — 'Key points', cancer sites, and 'Recommendations'; Child and Adolescent Immunization Schedule by Age (Compliant) — notice identifying the July 2, 2025 schedule as the current CDC schedule under the March 16, 2026 preliminary order.
source_claim_supported: CDC currently supports routine HPV vaccination at ages 11–12, a 2-dose 0 and 6–12 month series when initiated at ages 9–14 for immunocompetent persons, prevention of new HPV infection rather than treatment, and cancer-prevention benefit for both males and females.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's generic cancer-prevention statement into a current HPV counseling and schedule item. Currentness was reverified against CDC's 2026-compliant schedule status, and the stem specifies immunocompetent age 11 to exclude the 3-dose immunocompromised schedule.
audit_findings: Currentness was checked against CDC's compliant schedule page, which explicitly identifies the July 2, 2025 schedule as the current CDC child/adolescent schedule in 2026 under a March 16, 2026 court order.
The current CDC schedule notes routine HPV vaccination at 11–12 years and a 2-dose 0, 6–12 month series for initiation at ages 9–14.
The stem specifies immunocompetent status, excluding the special 3-dose schedule for immunocompromised persons.
CDC directly supports prevention of new infection, not treatment, and cancer relevance to both males and females.
Independent adversarial review found no schedule error, second answer, cueing, sex-specific misconception, locator defect, or unresolved currentness conflict.
